title: The bean field
hookLine: he hoed beans to know beans, and to learn patience (Walden 7)
last: A LIFE NEEDS ROOM ALONE, WITH ONE, WITH MANY.

cards: Early morning, a field near a pond, and a man with a hoe. The rows are long, the weeds are quick, and something keeps nibbling the young leaves overnight. He works through the dew until the sun gets high, then goes in.
Tomorrow, the same. A neighbor passing on the road might see nothing but a farmer's job, and not a very efficient one. Thoreau saw something else.
He gave this field a whole chapter of Walden, called The Bean-Field, and in it he says he was determined to know beans.

teach.b: First, the work itself. Thoreau describes his daily labor as making the earth "say beans instead of grass." It's a funny line, and an honest one.
The ground wanted to grow its own things; every morning he asked it to grow his. Second, the question he can't quite answer.
Why raise beans at all? He doesn't give a tidy reason. He grew to love his rows, he says, though there were more of them than he needed.
The love came from the doing, not from a plan. Third, the joke inside the title. In plain American speech, someone who doesn't know beans doesn't know much.
Thoreau turns it around: he spent a summer bent over one plant because he wanted to know beans, really know them, the way you only know something you've tended with your own hands.
Some people, he says, must work in fields so that a parable-maker will one day have words to use. He was farming and writing the parable at the same time. Fourth, the patience.
Beans don't hurry, and the field is never only yours.
He names his enemies plainly: "worms, cool days, and most of all woodchucks." But by the end of the chapter he softens.
He wonders whether the beans grow partly for the woodchucks, and writes, "These beans have results which are not harvested by me." The patience he learned wasn't just waiting.
It was letting the field belong to more than him.

how: Readers of Walden often take the bean field as a picture of slow, attentive work: tending something by hand until you know it, and accepting that what you grow is shared with more than you.

practice: Turn toward a plant near you, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a tree outside the window, or bring to mind one you've known, and look at it the way a person looks at something they mean to know: one leaf, its edge, where it's growing toward.
Notice that it's in no hurry at all. If you can, give it one small thing, a little water or a dead leaf removed, and then let it be.
